value.overview: The Rufous-necked Wood-Rail (Aramides axillaris) is a secretive rail of tropical forests, wetlands, mangroves, and dense vegetation. It spends much of its time walking on the ground rather than flying and is often detected by its loud, distinctive calls. The species occurs from Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America, including Costa Rica, where it is a resident associated mainly with suitable habitat on the Pacific side.
value.classification: The Rufous-necked Wood-Rail belongs to the rail family Rallidae and the order Gruiformes. It is one of the forest- and wetland-associated wood-rails in the genus Aramides.
value.identification: This medium-sized rail is about 38 cm long and has a long bill, long legs, and a relatively short tail. Adults show a gray head and throat, a rufous or cinnamon-colored neck, breast, and flanks, an olive-brown back, and blackish lower belly, rump, and tail. The bill is yellowish to greenish, the eyes are reddish, and the legs are coral-red. It can be confused with other wood-rails where ranges overlap; its strongly rufous neck and smaller, more compact appearance are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Rufous-necked Wood-Rail ranges from Mexico and Central America south through parts of northern and western South America, with additional populations on Trinidad. In Costa Rica it is reported mainly on the Pacific slope, where it is a resident and can be locally common. It occupies lowlands and foothills, reaching at least about 1,400 m, in riparian woodland, mangroves, swamps, shaded forest edges, secondary growth, and vegetated areas beside pastures or crops.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, the species occurs year-round in suitable Pacific-slope habitats; seasonal movements, if they occur, are likely local and have not been clearly established.
value.breeding: The nest is a bulky, compact structure made from dry leaves and twigs, usually placed about 2 to 3 m above the ground in a shrub, tangle, or climbing vegetation. A clutch typically contains three to five pale eggs marked with reddish or lilac-colored spots. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from approximately April through August or September, although timing may vary with local rainfall and habitat conditions.
value.dietFeeding: The Rufous-necked Wood-Rail forages mainly on the ground in leaf litter, mud, and dense vegetation. Its diet likely includes insects and other invertebrates, small crustaceans, seeds, and fallen plant material. It walks deliberately while probing and turning through cover, and may feed along muddy edges, in mangroves, or near streams and wet forest. Specific feeding observations are limited because the species is secretive.
value.behavior: Usually solitary or found in pairs, this wood-rail keeps to shaded, dense cover and is more often heard than seen. When disturbed, it commonly runs quickly through vegetation and only rarely flies. It may become easier to observe when approached quietly and patiently. Its loud calls are important for communication and may help reveal its presence in otherwise difficult-to-see forest-edge and wetland habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
